newsitem.title: MEXICO: Pemex eyeing U.S. West Coast contracts - trader.
newsitem.headline: Pemex eyeing U.S. West Coast contracts - trader.

text.p: Mexico's state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) is looking to revive crude exports along the West Coast, a Pemex trader said on Monday.
Mexico last exported to the West Coast in 1991, said the trader, who declined to be named.
"We've been trying, but there is still nothing firm," the trader said.
West coast traders said Pemex has been talking to potential heavy crude Maya buyers.
Pemex has been looking to increase refining activity and secure new crude contracts in efforts to disperse a greater quantity of Maya amid a glut in the Gulf of Mexico.

Mexico reached 2.968 million barrels per day of crude output in February, of which more than half was high sulphur Maya, with an API of 22. Pemex aims to boost crude exports 9.2 percent in 1997 from the previous year.
Meanwhile, international demand for the heavy Maya and for crude in general has slipped, while regional producers have also upped production.
Expanding Pemex's market to the West Coast from the Gulf of Mexico, the destination of the majority of Pemex's crude exports, may face physical limitations, the source said.
Exports to the West Coast are restricted by limited depth capacity at the nation's key Pacific Coast port, Salina Cruz, which currently handles shipments of about 90,000 barrels.
Pemex's oil tankers are typically built to handle between 700,000 and 1.9 million barrels.
